interest: For diplomatic and military historians, this file provides an invaluable, real-time chronicle of the decisive turning point in U.S.–Japanese relations during the spring and summer of 1941, seen directly through the eyes of the American Embassy in Tokyo. It offers firsthand, candid accounts of high-level diplomatic conferences between Ambassador Grew and Japanese leaders, capturing how Allied economic sanctions and asset freezes were perceived in Tokyo as an existential encirclement following the occupation of southern Indochina. Furthermore, the inclusion of granular economic data, records of domestic political upheavals (such as the purge of Matsuoka and the attempted assassination of Baron Hiranuma), and complete monthly schedules of telegrams and despatches provides researchers with an exceptional tool to reconstruct the Embassy’s daily information flow, crisis management, and reporting priorities on the brink of war.
overview: This file (File 1302, decimal file 894.00) spans March 24 through September 23, 1941, and documents the rapid deterioration of United States–Japanese relations in the critical months leading up to the Pacific War through comprehensive monthly political, military, and economic reports prepared by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and the staff of the American Embassy in Tokyo. Supplemented by internal State Department analytical memoranda, duplicate report copies, and detailed schedules of outgoing telegrams and despatches, the collection chronicles international flashpoints including Foreign Minister Yōsuke Matsuoka’s diplomacy resulting in the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, the diplomatic shock of Germany’s invasion of the USSR, Japan’s military occupation of southern French Indochina, the retaliatory freezing of Japanese assets and trade embargoes by the United States, Great Britain, and the Netherlands East Indies, and direct frictions such as the aerial bombing of the gunboat USS Tutuila at Chungking. Concurrently, the records trace Japan’s internal political and wartime economic transformation, highlighting the fall of the Second Konoe Cabinet to oust Matsuoka, the installation of the Third Konoe Cabinet, the attempted assassination of Baron Kiichirō Hiranuma, the reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, and intensifying domestic strain reflected in rationing and large-scale military mobilization.
